name: CBT-I

lead: CBT-I is a structured program that changes sleep-related habits and thoughts to treat chronic insomnia. People with long-running sleep problems use it to get consistent sleep again, and appearance communities connect that with healthier-looking skin, eyes and a less tired face.

It combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene to rebuild the association between bed and sleep. The American College of Physicians (2016) recommends it as initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, a 2015 meta-analysis reported benefits on diary measures of sleep, and digital versions have been tested in randomized trials. No studies link it to appearance.

paras: It is delivered over several weeks by a therapist, in groups, or through digital programs, with sleep diaries and a set bed and wake schedule. Many people notice improvement within the first weeks.
Sleep restriction can temporarily cause fatigue and daytime sleepiness. Some conditions, such as epilepsy or bipolar disorder, call for caution, so it is not suitable for everyone.

web.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia — Wikipedia
Treatment of chronic insomnia by restriction of time in bed

angle.text: CBT-I fixes chronic insomnia, giving more consistent sleep that people link to rested skin, eyes and a less tired face. It is the guideline-recommended first-line treatment for insomnia.

lead: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, multi-component program that retrains sleep habits and sleep-related thinking. Its core techniques are stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation training and sleep hygiene, and it can be delivered by a clinician, in groups, by telehealth, or through internet and app programs.[1][2]

People in looks, lifting and recovery communities turn to it because sleep is the base that skin, hair, body composition, training recovery and mood sit on. The chain they describe is straightforward: CBT-I targets chronic insomnia, steadier and more consolidated sleep follows without sleep medication, and rested people tend to look fresher around the eyes and face, train more consistently and keep their routines going. Forum users mention it as the drug-free route for people whose sleep is the bottleneck.[3][4]

The American College of Physicians (2016) recommends CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, and reviews in The Lancet and Primary Care describe it as the first-line option.[5][6][2] A 2015 meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials with 1,162 participants examined its effect on diary measures of sleep, and later meta-analyses have looked at internet and digital delivery and at insomnia occurring alongside depression, PTSD and other conditions.[7][8][9][10] Research on appearance outcomes specifically has not been published; the trials measure sleep, mood and related health outcomes.
infobox: Chronic insomnia (difficulty falling or staying asleep with daytime impact)
Stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation training, sleep hygiene[1]
Individual, group, telehealth, internet and app-based[1][8][9]
American College of Physicians 2016; American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2021[1][5]
Several weeks of structured sessions; sleep restriction can take weeks to months[1]

paras: CBT-I treats insomnia by changing the behaviors and beliefs that keep it going rather than by sedating the brain. The Lancet's 2022 review notes that insomnia occurs in up to 50 percent of primary care patients and that CBT-I is the recommended first-line treatment whether or not an underlying cause has been identified.[6] The Primary Care review of 2024 explains the 3P model of insomnia (predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating factors) and the hyperarousal during non-REM sleep that CBT-I aims to reduce.[2]

Wikipedia's overview of insomnia estimates that 10 to 30 percent of adults have insomnia at any given time and that around 6 percent have insomnia lasting over a month that is not explained by another problem. It describes CBT-I as the first-line treatment, with benefits that persist after therapy ends, and notes that it demands time and motivation.[11] A person who is a candidate for CBT-I typically has trouble falling or staying asleep that causes distress or daytime impairment, and not primarily a circadian rhythm disorder or an unstable medical illness.[1]

sections.h: How CBT-I can matter for appearance
paras: People who care about how they look usually reach CBT-I through a recovery question: what to do when sleep, rather than diet or training, is the limiting factor. The chain they describe runs from sleep to recovery to physique and presentation. Longer, more consolidated sleep is associated in their discussions with steadier energy for training, a more regular routine, better mood, and a more rested look in the skin and around the eyes.[3][4]

What the research literature measures is different. The randomized trials and meta-analyses of CBT-I report sleep onset latency, time awake after sleep onset, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, insomnia severity, remission, depression and anxiety outcomes.[7][12][10][13] Studies of how CBT-I changes skin, facial appearance or body composition have not been published, so the appearance link rests on the general role of sleep rather than on CBT-I-specific trials.

Wikipedia's article presents the program as a combination of behavioral methods (stimulus control, sleep scheduling and relaxation) with cognitive work on sleep-related worry. It presents the package as having been assembled from those behavioral and cognitive strands.[1]

The key early paper for sleep restriction is the 1987 report in the journal Sleep by Arthur Spielman, Paul Saskin and Michael Thorpy, who proposed that excess time in bed helps sustain chronic insomnia.[14] Charles Morin's 1993 book Insomnia: Psychological Assessment and Management and his later reviews of non-drug insomnia treatments (1999 and 2006, the latter with Bootzin, Buysse, Edinger, Espie and Lichstein) are the standard references cited for the integrated program.[1] Espie and colleagues' work from 2012 is among the trials of computerized delivery that Wikipedia cites.[1]

Guideline endorsement followed. The American College of Physicians published its recommendation of CBT-I as the initial treatment in 2016, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2021 guideline on behavioral and psychological treatments is also cited in the Wikipedia article.[1][5] In 2020 a task force of the European CBT-I Academy published practical recommendations for sleep problems during COVID-19 home confinement, an example of the program being adapted for public use.[15]

Stimulus control tries to rebuild the link between the bed and sleep. Typical instructions include using the bed only for sleep, keeping a consistent rising time and leaving the bed after roughly twenty minutes awake.[1]

Stimulus control stems from the behavioral tradition of treating insomnia as a conditioned response in which the bed and bedroom become cues for wakefulness. The Wikipedia summary lists the usual instructions as going to bed only when sleepy, keeping the bed for sleep and sex, keeping a fixed wake time, and leaving the bed if sleep has not come after about 20 minutes.[1]
Sleep restriction temporarily limits time in bed to match actual sleep, then extends it gradually as sleep efficiency improves. Clinicians describe it as the most demanding step.[1]

In the original 1987 report by Spielman, Saskin and Thorpy, 35 patients with a mean insomnia history of 15.4 years had their time in bed sharply restricted and then gradually extended as sleep efficiency improved. After eight weeks they reported longer total sleep, shorter time to fall asleep and less time awake, and a subset followed up about 36 weeks later still showed gains; the authors noted that some patients found the schedule hard to keep.[14] Wikipedia describes modern protocols as starting with a time in bed of at least about five hours and adjusting it weekly by 20 to 30 minutes depending on sleep efficiency.[1]

subs.h: Cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene
paras: Cognitive therapy addresses beliefs such as expecting to be wrecked after one short night. Relaxation training, including meditation or guided imagery, helps mainly with falling asleep, and sleep hygiene covers caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and the sleep environment.[1] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline recommends against sleep hygiene as a stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia.[1]
A 2024 component network meta-analysis in JAMA Psychiatry set out to estimate the contribution of each component and delivery format to remission in randomized trials.[12]

Wikipedia also lists paradoxical intention (deliberately trying to stay awake to reduce performance anxiety), biofeedback and a roughly two-week sleep diary used for assessment among the tools that clinicians draw on.[1] Acceptance and commitment therapy and mindfulness are described as complements, with a 2014 study reporting help for some people who had not responded to CBT-I.[1]

CBT-I can be delivered face to face, in groups, through telehealth or via internet and app programs.[1] Meta-analyses of internet-delivered and digital CBT-I reported efficacy in randomized trials, which has widened access.[8][9] A narrative review in the Journal of General Internal Medicine examined ways of increasing access to and use of CBT-I, and its authors discuss the limited number of trained providers.[16] Wikipedia notes that technology-mediated treatment works best when adherence is high.[1]

An app-based CBT-I trial in young people with insomnia and subclinical depression was published in PLoS Medicine in 2025, and a separate randomized trial of CBT-based chatbots examined insomnia, depression and anxiety symptoms.[17][18] Hacker News has carried several Show HN posts for CBT-I apps and AI sleep coaches, reflecting developer interest in the format.[19]

The 2015 Annals of Internal Medicine meta-analysis pooled 20 randomized trials of face-to-face multimodal CBT-I against inactive comparators in adults with chronic insomnia without comorbidities, and measured sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time and sleep efficiency.[7] The Lancet review reports that CBT-I and sleep medication have similar acute effects, but only CBT-I has shown durable benefit after treatment ends.[6] Wikipedia summarises one comparison against zopiclone in older adults in which CBT-I gave more deep sleep and less time awake, with benefits holding at six months, and a comparison against zolpidem in which CBT-I had a larger effect on sleep-onset insomnia and adding the drug did not improve on CBT-I alone.[1]

Wikipedia's article suggests that stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive therapy are the most effective components, and that a 2023 systematic review found stimulus control and sleep restriction together produced gains similar to full CBT-I in older adults in as few as two sessions.[1] The 2024 JAMA Psychiatry component network meta-analysis set out to estimate the contribution of each component and delivery format to remission.[12] A 2025 BMJ non-inferiority trial compared tai chi with CBT-I in middle-aged and older adults with insomnia.[20]

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline recommends against sleep hygiene as a stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia, while its advice remains a standard part of the full program.[1] Wikipedia also notes that CBT-I trials have enrolled mostly non-Hispanic White participants, which limits how far results generalize.[1]

Insomnia often appears with other conditions. A JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis examined CBT-I in people with psychiatric and medical comorbidity, and a 2022 Sleep Medicine Reviews meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials looked at CBT-I in patients with mental disorders including depression, PTSD, alcohol dependence, bipolar disorder and psychosis.[21][10] Randomized trials have studied CBT-I for preventing depression in older adults and in youth, and for people who have both insomnia and depression.[17][13][22][23] A systematic review of trials in cancer survivors, who commonly have insomnia, was published in 2016, and Wikipedia describes CBT-I as the most effective non-drug option in that group.[1][24]

sections.h: How it compares with sleeping pills
paras: Wikipedia describes CBT-I as probably more effective and acceptable than medication because it changes sleep habits and thought patterns rather than sedating the patient.[1] Its insomnia article says medications are second-line, mainly for short-term use, and that sleep restriction and other CBT-I effects last after therapy ends.[11] A comparative-effectiveness systematic review in BMC Family Practice examined CBT-I against other treatments.[25] Wikipedia says sleep restriction can take several weeks or months to complete, and that one expert suggests reaching 7 to 8 hours of sleep within about six weeks.[1]

Sleep restriction can cause fatigue, sleepiness, headaches, irritability and appetite changes, usually in the first one to two weeks. It is not recommended where drowsiness would be unsafe, such as operating heavy machinery, and may worsen epilepsy. Relaxation training can cause paradoxical anxiety in some patients, stimulus control can be hazardous for people at high risk of falls, and CBT-I in bipolar disorder may raise the risk of switching to mania.[1]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and recovery communities
paras: Lifters and appearance-focused posters treat sleep as the base layer under skin, body composition, hormones and training recovery, and some name CBT-I as the non-drug option when insomnia is the problem rather than habits alone.[3][4] On T Nation, a thread about nights of poor sleep lists behavioral measures alongside supplements and medication, and one member who completed professional CBT-I training says the most important lessons concerned habits such as not watching the clock.[3][26] Another thread on insomnia during testosterone therapy has a member describing a costly path through sleep specialists that ended in a prescription and a CPAP.[27]

Users who see low energy or low-testosterone symptoms suggest CBT-I as a non-drug step for people in their thirties whose labs are otherwise normal.[4] Hacker News posts show CBT-I being packaged into apps and AI coaches for self-optimizers.[19] The chain people describe is: fewer sleepless nights, better recovery and routine, and a fresher look, although studies of CBT-I have measured sleep and mood outcomes, not appearance.[7][6]

The 2015 Annals meta-analysis covered 20 trials (1,162 participants, mean age 56) of face-to-face CBT-I in chronic insomnia without comorbidities.[7] The ACP guideline of 2016 rested on a systematic review of randomized trials published from 2004 to 2015 and recommended CBT-I as initial treatment.[5] The 1987 sleep restriction study followed 35 patients and reported gains at eight weeks that persisted in those followed to about 36 weeks.[14]

For insomnia alongside other conditions, a JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis examined psychiatric and medical comorbidity, and a 2022 Sleep Medicine Reviews meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials looked at CBT-I in patients with mental disorders, measuring insomnia severity and mental health.[21][10] A JAMA Psychiatry trial studied prevention of incident and recurrent major depression in older adults with insomnia, and a 2024 double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial examined psychological treatment of comorbid insomnia and depression.[13][22] Internet-based and digital CBT-I have been evaluated in meta-analyses of randomized trials.[8][9] No studies of CBT-I for appearance outcomes such as skin or facial look were found.

CBT-I forms part of the wider shift in sleep medicine toward behavioral treatment before medication. A T Nation post quoting sleep drug guidance notes that guidelines recommend prescription sleep drugs only after CBT-I and behavioral changes have been tried.[28] On T Nation, members who trained in CBT-I or who recommend it describe habits such as not watching the clock and keeping a fixed schedule.[3][26] Others in the strength community suggest it to people with low energy or low testosterone symptoms as a non-drug option.[4]
A 2023 editorial in the journal Sleep, titled 'CBT-I: what is next?', reflects ongoing discussion in the field about the program's future directions.[29]

lore.intro: CBT-I appears in strength, recovery and looks discussions as the structured, non-pharmaceutical answer to poor sleep, and in tech circles as a product category for apps and AI coaches.[3][4][19]
